title: Worth something alone
hook: A network app gets some value even with nobody else on it. Is that enough to start?

doesNotKnow: that some value with no other users shrinks the critical mass but leaves an empty app stuck at zero unless that value beats the price

misconception: Any value on its own is enough to get a network product started from zero.
objective: The learner can explain that stand-alone value below the price lowers the tipping point (20.0% to 7.3% at 10¢) but leaves a launch from 0 at 0%, because even the keenest fan values an empty app below the price, and that stand-alone value above the price (20¢) lets the app climb from 0 to about 85%.

claims.text: In this toy market person x (from 0, the keenest, to 1) values the app at (1 - x) times (stand-alone value + share of people using it); the price is 16¢, and each round everyone who values it above 16¢ uses it, so next round's share is 1 - 0.16 / (stand-alone value + share), or 0.
claims.source: Model rules adopted by the lesson, extending the below-critical-mass toy market (economics/below-critical-mass c1) with a stand-alone value a. next() in src/demos/economics/worth-something-alone/Demo.tsx. The question's 'worth 10¢ to its keenest fan even with no other users' is the case a = 10¢ (x = 0, share 0). Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: With 10¢ of stand-alone value at a 16¢ price, a launch from 0 users stays at 0%, and the tipping point falls from 20.0% (no stand-alone value) to 7.3% (other resting point 82.7%).
claims.source: Resting shares solve (1 - z)(a + z) = 0.16: a = 0 gives 0.2 and 0.8; a = 0.1 gives z = (0.9 -+ sqrt(0.57))/2 = 0.0725 and 0.8275. At z = 0 with a = 0.1, next = max(0, 1 - 0.16/0.1) = 0. Builder's node run of crossings()/launch() in Demo.tsx: a = 0: 20.00, 80.00, launch 0, 0; a = 0.1: 7.25, 82.75, launch 0, 0. Brief check J11 (node company/courses/ncm/checks/rejudged-four.mjs): equilibria [0.073, 0.827], fromZero all 0. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: With 20¢ of stand-alone value, 0% is not a resting point: a launch from 0 goes 0, 20, 60, 80, 84 ... and settles at about 85% (84.7%).
claims.source: next(0.2, z) = 1 - 0.16/(0.2 + z): 0 -> 0.2 -> 0.6 -> 0.8 -> 0.84 -> 0.8462 -> 0.8471 (builder's node run of launch(); stops when a round moves under 0.1 point). Fixed point: z^2 - 0.8z - 0.04 = 0, z = 0.8472. J11 a = 0.2: equilibria [0.847], fromZero 0, 0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 0.84, 0.846. The stage rounds the share to whole percent (85%). Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: An empty network product sells to nobody unless someone's value with no other users exceeds the price: at 10¢ alone, even the keenest fan values an empty app below the 16¢ price; at 20¢ alone the first buyers come with nobody else on it.
claims.source: At share 0 the keenest person (x = 0) values the app at a, and everyone else at less, so the first round's share is positive only if a > price (next(a, 0) = max(0, 1 - 0.16/a)). On the stage this is the curve's left end (marked 'empty app') sitting below or above the price line. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: Stand-alone value lowers the critical mass, but removes the trap only when it beats the price.
claims.source: The tipping point is the lower root of (1 - z)(a + z) = 0.16, which falls as a rises (0.2 at a = 0, 0.0725 at a = 0.1) and is gone once a > 0.16, when share 0 stops being a resting point (c2, c4). The model is the lesson's (c6). Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: The model and numbers are invented for the lesson (a network value mixed with an individual one, the idea the book discusses in ch. 17) and are not a forecast for any real product.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 17 (section 17.6 unconfirmed). Stated modelling assumption; the card names no real product.

claims.text: On the chart, the curve is the value of the keenest person not yet using the app at each share; where it is above the price line the share grows, where it is below it shrinks, and the crossings are the shares where a round changes nothing.
claims.source: At share z the users are x < z, so the keenest non-user is x = z, valuing it (1 - z)(a + z). Next share > z exactly when 1 - 0.16/(a + z) > z, i.e. (1 - z)(a + z) > 0.16 (for a + z > 0). Builder-written; unverified. recall.question: A new messaging app is useful to its keenest fan even alone, but less than its price. It launches with no users. What happens?
options: Nobody joins, though it needs fewer users than before to take off
It grows slowly from its keenest fans
It takes off, because it is useful on its own
recall.why: With nobody else on it, even the keenest fan values it below the price, so no one starts. The stand-alone value lowers the critical mass, but only value above the price gets an empty app going.
